notes.body: The chapter builds toward this on its own: the Master tells the boy to hold fast "until you are guided by a rope from God to the rope of God." So there are apparently two different ropes, and the boy sensibly asks which is which. But then the Imam is called only "its outward sign" — the sign of something else — and when the boy asks the direct question, the answer is "That is the end of your guidance and the utmost of the worlds," which names neither rope. I am left unable to tell what the rope of God is as opposed to the rope from God, even though the whole passage turns on their being two things. The distinction is used to guide the boy and then withheld from him, and from me.
notes.quote: Then what is the rope of God, and what is the rope that comes from God?

notes.body: The Master unpacks the king's dream by naming, in one breath, 'the causes of God,' 'the seven appointed speakers,' and 'the guardians,' as if each were an already-familiar rank. But nowhere in the chapter is a 'cause of God' explained. Are these persons, offices, angelic beings? The word arrives fully loaded and is never opened. A first-time reader can follow that cows map to one thing and lean cows to another, but cannot tell WHAT the mapped-to things actually are, so the interpretation resolves one mystery into a set of new undefined ones. I would want to ask: what is a 'cause of God,' and how does it differ from a speaker or a guardian?
notes.quote: they are the causes of God that stand between Him and His creation

notes.body: The boy asks what the seven-eared grain is 'among us,' and the Master answers that it lies 'in the foundation of Islam, and its child is like a grain that sprouted seven ears — meaning that seven imams came out of his loins.' I could not fix the referents. Who is 'the foundation of Islam' — a person, an era, a first Imam? Whose child, and then whose loins does the closing 'his' point back to? The pronouns slide from an abstract 'foundation' to a 'child' to a masculine 'his loins' without a stable named subject, and the chapter never lands them on anyone I can identify. It reads as though I am expected to already know the figure being described.
notes.anchor: foundation of Islam and its child
notes.quote: its child is like a grain that sprouted seven ears
